title: Mary's song (Luke 1:46–55)
hookLine: she sings of a God who lifts the lowly and sends the rich away empty

cards: Still in Elizabeth's house, in the hills. Elizabeth has just blessed her, and you might expect Mary to say something modest. Thank you.
I don't know what's happening either. Instead, Luke gives her a song. Ten verses, and it isn't a lullaby.
It starts with thanks, turns to her own small life, and then, without warning, turns the whole world over. Thrones emptied. Hungry people fed.

Rich people walking away with nothing. A young woman from a small village, pregnant and not yet married, singing about the powerful coming down. Churches have sung her song at daily prayer for many centuries.

teach.h: MY SOUL DOTH MAGNIFY THE LORD.
teach.b: It begins: "My soul doth magnify the Lord, And my spirit hath rejoiced in God my Saviour." In the old Latin Bible the first word is Magnificat, magnifies, and that's the song's name.
To magnify is to make bigger: not to make God bigger, but big in your own eyes, the way a magnifying glass makes something small easy to see. Then Mary looks at herself.
God has noticed the low estate of his servant girl, she says, and from now on every generation will call her blessed. Then the song turns outward.
"He hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree. He hath filled the hungry with good things; and the rich he hath sent empty away." Notice the tense.

teach.h: SHE SINGS AS IF IT'S DONE.
teach.b: She sings as if it has already happened, the way the Hebrew prophets sometimes spoke of what they were sure was coming. And it echoes an older song.
In the book of Samuel, Hannah, who also waited for a child, sings something very close: God raises the poor from the dust. Mary sings in her people's words, in the line of the women before her.

teach.h: SUNG AT EVENING AND MORNING PRAYER.
teach.b: Catholics sing her song at evening prayer, Anglicans at Evensong, Lutherans at vespers. Orthodox Christians sing it in the morning service, with a hymn honoring Mary between the verses.
Catholics and Orthodox hear it as the song of the Mother of God; many Protestants hear a model of praise, and a warning to anyone comfortable.
All of them sing the same promise: the lowly are lifted.

how: The Magnificat is sung or said every evening in Catholic vespers and in Anglican Evening Prayer, and at Lutheran vespers; Orthodox churches sing it at the morning service, with a hymn to Mary as a refrain.

o: Latin for magnifies: Mary's song of praise
a Latin blessing said over a newborn
Mary's lullaby for the baby Jesus

games.q: what's inside the song — tap the pairs.

s: the Magnificat is a lullaby Mary sang to the baby Jesus
she sings it at Elizabeth's house, months before the birth, and it's about God turning the world over.
Mary's song echoes an older song by Hannah
in the book of Samuel, Hannah sings that God raises the poor from the dust.
only one church sings the Magnificat
Catholics, Anglicans, Lutherans and Orthodox Christians all sing it, at evening or morning prayer.

games.q: you're Mary. your older relative has just blessed you at her door. what comes out of your mouth?
o: a quiet thank you, and a question about what happens next.
a song about God lifting the lowly and emptying thrones.
a worried list of what people back home will say.
games.why: she sings: my soul doth magnify the Lord. and the song ends with the mighty put down and the hungry filled.

practice: Mary's song starts with thanks, so look back over the last few days for one small thing to be grateful for: someone who made room for you, a meal, a morning that went right.
Put it in one line of your own words, a sentence you'd actually say, and write it down if you can. If you pray, offer it as thanks; if you don't, just let it be true.

wordCard.voice: Magnificat. Latin for magnifies: the first word of Mary's song, where the mighty come down and the lowly are lifted.

orig.note: Greek: makes great, magnifies. the first word of Mary's song in Luke's Greek; Latin made it magnificat.
